column3: It joins divine knowledge of heaven and earth with disbelief in Allah and the designation of the disbelievers as losers.
It directly affirms Allah's dominion over heaven and earth, supporting the scope of the keys.
The mention of garlanded offerings only gives a lexical echo of keys and does not clarify the focus claim.
It repeats that Allah possesses the keys of heaven and earth and explains them through His governance of provision.
The immediately preceding ayah grounds the keys in Allah's creation of everything and guardianship over it.
Divine administration from heaven to earth gives a concrete expression of the authority summarized by the keys.
Creation of heaven and earth, followed by disbelief, closely supports both the sovereignty and rejection themes.
Its assertion that none can mislead one guided by Allah offers only a nearby affirmation of His exclusive power.
Allah's possession of all in heaven and earth and the return of affairs support comprehensive sovereignty.
It directly treats disbelief in Allah's signs, though its consequence is despair and punishment rather than loss.
Allah's exclusive knowledge of what is hidden in heaven and earth is a limited aspect of His comprehensive authority.
The kingdom of heaven and earth shown to Abraham supports the cosmic scope of divine dominion.
It explicitly assigns dominion over heaven and earth to Allah and adds the return of all affairs to Him.
The challenge to act and await the outcome does not clarify the keys, signs, or the stated loss.
It contrasts belief in revelation with denying Allah's signs, directly supporting the focus's second clause.
Allah's dominion over heaven and earth and witness over all things supports the authority implied by the keys.
The purposive creation of heaven and earth supports their being under meaningful divine control.
It identifies disbelief in the signs as a defining condition, though without the focus's language of loss.
It calls covenant-breakers who sever what Allah ordered joined losers, a related account of loss through rejection.
The sufficiency of Allah against feared rivals supports exclusive reliance, but not the keys or signs directly.
Its description of Cain becoming a loser shares only the consequence, in a distinct moral narrative.
Forgetting Allah under satanic influence culminates in being losers, a related account of spiritual loss.
It states that heaven and earth were created in truth, supporting the purposeful order behind divine possession.
Allah's knowledge of what is in heaven and earth supports the universal scope of His authority.
It pairs the true creation of heaven and earth with people turning away from warning.
The contrast between guidance and self-harming error relates broadly to the focus's warning about disbelief and loss.
The universal statement that humanity is in loss is too general to illuminate the focus's stated cause.
It expressly warns that denying Allah's signs makes one of the losers.
The book's descent from Allah supports revealed signs only indirectly.
Calling those secure from Allah's plan losers has a related consequence but a different grounds for it.
It identifies the disbelievers as the losers in the Hereafter, reinforcing the focus's outcome.
The threatened enduring punishment is a nearby consequence but has no direct link to keys or signs.
A false assumption about the Lord leads directly to becoming losers, explaining a related path to loss.
It connects disbelief in the Lord's signs with painful punishment, closely supporting the warning in the focus.
Allah's exclusive knowledge of the unseen in heaven and earth is only one limited aspect of the keys.
The oath by the heaven and its construction supports creation but not possession, signs, or loss.
All who are in heaven and earth belong to Allah and obey Him, supporting universal dominion.
It states that all intercession and dominion over heaven and earth belong to Allah, immediately anticipating the focus.
Its generic statement that an event is a sign does not substantially clarify the focus.
It gives a historical pattern in which people disbelieve in Allah's signs and are seized for their sins.
The nearby rejection of powerless intercessors supports exclusive divine authority only indirectly.
Calling Allah Lord of heaven, earth, and what lies between reinforces the scope of His sovereignty.
Its separation of evil from good ends with losers but does not explain the focus's signs or keys.
All in heaven and earth glorify Allah as King, Holy, Mighty, and Wise, reinforcing universal kingship.
The disbelievers' response to the summons does not materially illuminate the focus claim.
Allah's possession of all in heaven and earth refutes divided divine status and supports exclusive dominion.
Provision being expanded and restricted is a related local expression of Allah's authority and signs.
The image of disbelievers rushing toward the Messenger is not a useful link to the focus.
Believers' faith in their Lord's signs provides the positive counterpart to the focus's disbelief.
The duration formula involving heaven and earth does not clarify authority over them or disbelief in signs.
It identifies persistent disbelievers as those who do not believe, supporting the focus's warning about rejection.
It assigns all in heaven and earth and abiding religion to Allah, reinforcing exclusive possession and devotion.
Its affirmation of Allah as One and Overpowering rejects association, but only indirectly supports the focus.
No one can escape Allah in earth or heaven, expressing the inescapable reach of His authority.
Allah's grandeur in heaven and earth is a close attribute-level parallel to the focus's comprehensive sovereignty.
Allah's possession of heaven and earth and complete knowledge reinforce the extent of His authority.
It explicitly makes association lead to ruined works and being among the losers, in the focus's immediate context.
It combines Allah's dominion over heaven and earth with the loss of those devoted to falsehood.
The preceding argument from creation of heaven and earth to the helplessness of rivals prepares the focus's exclusive keys.
It identifies a condemned community as losers, a related consequence without the focus's specific ground.
It links disbelief and denial of Allah's signs to the Fire, closely supporting the focus's warning.
The duration formula involving heaven and earth does not clarify the focus's authority or rejection themes.
Creator names and the praise of all in heaven and earth support divine sovereignty at a general level.
It links disbelief and denial of Allah's signs to the Fire, closely supporting the focus's warning.
Its life, death, and sleep signs offer a nearby example of divine control but not the focus's main relation.
Allah's possession of heaven and earth and encompassing knowledge support the scope of the keys.
It identifies those who do not believe in Allah's signs as fabricators, reinforcing the moral character of rejection.
Its household privacy instruction and closing reference to signs do not meaningfully clarify the focus.
Calling despairing people disbelievers shares only a broad rejection theme.
It calls those who worship apart from Allah the manifest losers, a direct nearby account of the focus's loss.
The statement of greater punishment gives no useful connection to keys, signs, or loss.
It assigns Allah dominion over heaven and earth, denies any partner, and affirms measured creation.
It calls those whom Allah leaves astray losers, a related contrast between divine guidance and loss.
The invitation to observe the spread earth is only a limited creation-side parallel.
Creation of heaven and earth in truth is itself called a sign for believers, linking both major themes.
Allah's possession of all in heaven and earth supports the comprehensive scope of the keys.
The invitation to observe the raised heaven supports cosmic reflection only broadly.
It records outright disbelief in the reminder, a concise parallel to rejecting divine signs.
It contrasts proper belief in the Book with disbelief in it and explicitly calls the latter group losers.
It makes denial of Allah's signs the reason for the enduring Fire, reinforcing the focus's warning.
It pairs creation of heaven and earth in truth with Allah's transcendence over what people associate with Him.
All that is in heaven and earth belongs to Allah, directly supporting the focus's scope of possession.
It connects disbelief and denial of signs with the Fire, a related consequence to the focus's loss.
Its criticism of empty worship and disbelief is a distant connection to the focus's rejection theme.
It contrasts faith with disbelief and denial of signs, assigning the latter to the Fire.
It describes the nullification of disbelievers' deeds but does not connect this to signs or cosmic authority.
It assigns all in heaven and earth to Allah and warns disbelievers of severe punishment.
Its rhetorical denial that the opponents created heaven and earth directly supports exclusive divine creative authority.
It asks who owns all in heaven and earth, answers Allah, and joins disbelief to losing oneself.
The warning of a punishment from heaven concerns divine power but not the focus's keys or signs.
The curse upon those who die in disbelief shares only the broad consequence of rejection.
Human dispersal on earth and eventual gathering are only a distant expression of divine control.
Clear signs recited by the Messenger bring believers from darkness to light, supplying the positive response to signs.
The stripping of the heaven is an eschatological image with little direct relation to the focus.
It challenges alleged partners to show what they created on earth or their share in heaven, directly confirming exclusive authority.
It says that even every sign will not produce belief in some people, directly illustrating stubborn rejection of signs.
The revelation formula supports the source of signs only indirectly.
Reviving the earth and making signs clear is a general example of signs, not a close parallel.
It depicts people who see every sign yet refuse belief, directly illustrating the focus's disbelief in signs.
The earth illuminated for final judgment is a nearby eschatological setting but not a close thematic parallel.
It magnifies Allah's unmatched power by placing the whole earth in His grasp and the heavens folded in His hand, a major expansion of the keys motif.
The immediate command rejecting worship of others applies the exclusive authority affirmed by the keys.
It draws the practical conclusion of the surrounding passage: worship Allah alone and be among the grateful.
It describes Allah's creation of heaven and earth and His ordering of cosmic cycles, grounding the authority asserted in the focus.
It explicitly assigns Allah the dominion of heaven, earth, and all within them, a direct parallel to the keys' scope.
It states that dominion over heaven and earth belongs to Allah and that He has power over everything.
It twice assigns all in heaven and earth to Allah, strongly reinforcing universal possession.
It links Allah's dominion over heaven and earth to the absence of any protector or helper apart from Him.
Allah's throne encompasses heaven and earth and their preservation does not burden Him, closely supporting comprehensive authority.
It assigns all in heaven and earth to Allah and joins that ownership to final accounting.
It gives Allah possession of all in heaven and earth and returns all matters to Him.
It assigns all in heaven and earth to Allah and connects this to His forgiveness and punishment.
It names Allah as God in heaven and on earth and contrasts His knowledge with human action.
It states that Allah created heaven and earth in truth and that His command is truth.
It joins creation of heaven and earth with Allah's command and governance of the cosmos.
It explicitly assigns Allah dominion over heaven and earth and calls people to believe in Him and His signs.
It states that Allah alone has the dominion of heaven and earth and gives life and death.
Its questions about provision from heaven and earth, hearing, sight, life, and governance directly unpack divine control.
It asserts that all in heaven and earth belongs to Allah and that His promise is true.
It assigns all beings in heaven and earth to Allah and denies that alleged partners have real standing.
It asks who is Lord of heaven and earth, answers Allah, and challenges the supposed equals people take besides Him.
It presents all in heaven and earth as prostrating to Allah, expressing universal submission to His authority.
It states that Allah created heaven and earth in truth and can replace people if He wills.
It depicts every creature in heaven and earth prostrating to Allah, reinforcing total divine lordship.
It says the seven heavens, earth, and all within them glorify Allah, supporting the focus's cosmic scope.
It argues from Allah's creation of heaven and earth to His power to recreate humanity.
Allah is called Lord of heaven, earth, and what lies between them, followed by the command to worship Him steadfastly.
It assigns to Allah what is in heaven, earth, between them, and beneath the soil.
It denies that Allah created heaven, earth, and what lies between them in play, affirming purposeful creation.
It assigns all in heaven and earth to Allah and depicts those near Him as never weary of worship.
It argues that multiple gods in heaven and earth would have corrupted them, directly defending undivided sovereignty.
It identifies Allah as Lord of heaven, earth, and what lies between them, the One worshipped by Abraham.
It asks who owns the earth and all within it, eliciting the acknowledgement that it belongs to Allah.
It follows by asking who is Lord of the seven heavens and the mighty throne, eliciting the same acknowledgement.
It asks who holds sovereignty over everything and protects while none can protect against Him, closely explaining the keys.
It depicts all in heaven and earth, including birds, as knowing their prayer and glorification of Allah.
It identifies Allah as Creator of heaven, earth, and what lies between them and calls people to know Him.
It calls Allah Lord of heaven, earth, and what lies between them for those who have certainty.
It asks whether alleged gods created heaven and earth and sent down water, directly refuting rivals to Allah's authority.
It records the opponents' admission that Allah created heaven and earth and subjected the sun and moon, then exposes their inconsistency.
It similarly records the admission that Allah created heaven and earth and questions why people turn away.
It presents Allah as Creator of heaven, earth, and what lies between them and asks whether people will reflect.
It gives Allah praise and possession of all in heaven and earth, together with His wisdom and awareness.
It praises Allah as Creator of heaven and earth, who appoints angels as messengers.
It states that Allah holds heaven and earth lest they pass away, a vivid expression of sustaining authority.
It argues that the Creator of heaven and earth is fully able to create humanity again.
It calls Allah Lord of the heavens, earth, and what lies between them, and Lord of the rising points.
It treats the creation of heaven and earth as greater than the creation of humanity, reinforcing divine power.
It calls the creation and dispersal of beings in heaven and earth signs of Allah's power to gather them.
It records the admission that the Mighty, Knowing One created heaven and earth, exposing the contradiction of association.
It blesses the One to whom belongs the dominion of heaven, earth, and what lies between them.
It states that Allah created heaven and earth in truth so every soul may be repaid for what it earned.
It argues that the Creator of heaven and earth, unfatigued by their creation, can give life to the dead.
It affirms the creation of heaven, earth, and what lies between them without fatigue.
It assigns to Allah all that is in heaven and earth and connects it to requital for deeds.
It assigns Allah dominion over heaven and earth and describes Him as giving life, causing death, and having power over all things.
It states that all in heaven and earth glorifies Allah, the Mighty and Wise.
It assigns Allah dominion over heaven and earth, says all glorifies Him, and affirms His power over everything.
It describes Allah's creation of seven heavens and of earths like them, with His command descending among them.
